title: Chapter 38 — Conclusion
paragraphs: Reader, I married him. A quiet wedding we had—just he and I, the parson, and the clerk. When we got back from church, I went into the kitchen of the manor house, where Mary was cooking dinner and John cleaning the knives, and I said—

"Mary, I married Mr. Rochester this morning." The housekeeper and her husband were both the kind of calm, steady people to whom you can safely announce remarkable news without having your ears pierced by a shriek or your head stunned by a flood of amazed chatter. Mary did look up, and she did stare at me. The ladle she was using to baste a pair of roasting chickens hung suspended in midair for about three minutes, and for that same span John's knives also went still, resting from their polishing. But Mary, bending again over the roast, said only—
"Have you, Miss? Well, I never!"

A short time later she added: "I saw you go out with the master, but I didn't know you'd gone to church to be married." And she went back to her basting. John, when I turned to him, was grinning from ear to ear.

"I told Mary how it would be," he said. "I knew what Mr. Edward"—John was an old servant who had known his master since boyhood, so he often used his first name—"I knew what Mr. Edward would do. And I was certain he wouldn't wait long either. And he's done right, in my opinion. I wish you joy, Miss!" And he politely touched his forehead.

"Thank you, John. Mr. Rochester told me to give you and Mary this." I pressed a five-pound note into his hand. Without waiting to hear more, I left the kitchen. Passing the door a short while later, I caught the words—

"She'll likely do better for him than any of the grand ladies would have." And again: "If she's not one of the handsomest, she's no fool and very good-natured. And in his eyes she's beautiful—anyone can see that."

I wrote to Moor House and to Cambridge immediately, explaining what I had done and fully laying out my reasons. Diana and Mary approved the step without reservation. Diana announced she would give me time to finish the honeymoon, and then she would come and see me.

"She'd better not wait that long, Jane," said Mr. Rochester when I read her letter to him. "If she does, she'll be too late—for our honeymoon will last our whole lives. Its light will only fade over your grave or mine."

How St. John received the news, I don't know. He never answered the letter in which I told him. Yet six months later he wrote to me—without, however, mentioning Mr. Rochester's name or my marriage. His letter was calm and, though very serious, kind. He has kept up a regular, if not frequent, correspondence ever since. He hopes I am happy and trusts I am not among those who live without God in the world and think only of earthly things.

You haven't quite forgotten little Adèle, have you, reader? I hadn't. I soon asked and received permission from Mr. Rochester to go and see her at the school where he had placed her. Her wild joy at seeing me again moved me deeply. She looked pale and thin. She said she was not happy. I found that the rules of the school were too strict and its course of study too demanding for a child her age, so I took her home with me. I meant to become her governess once more, but I soon found that impossible—my time and care were now required by another; my husband needed them all. So I found a school run on a gentler system, and near enough that I could visit her often and bring her home sometimes. I made sure she never lacked for anything that could add to her comfort. She soon settled into her new home, grew very happy there, and made good progress in her studies. As she grew up, a solid English education corrected, to a great extent, the faults of her French upbringing, and by the time she left school I found in her a pleasant and obliging companion: docile, good-tempered, and well-principled. Through her grateful attentiveness to me and mine, she has long since more than repaid whatever small kindness I was ever able to show her.
My story draws near its close. One word about my experience of married life, and one brief glance at the fortunes of those whose names have appeared most often in this narrative, and I am done.

I have now been married ten years. I know what it is to live entirely for and with the person I love most on earth. I consider myself supremely blessed—blessed beyond what words can express—because I am my husband's life as fully as he is mine. No woman was ever nearer to her husband than I am—never was any woman more truly bone of his bone and flesh of his flesh. I never tire of my Edward's company; he never tires of mine, any more than we each tire of the heartbeat in our own chests. We are always together. To be together is for us to be at once as free as if we were alone, and as lighthearted as if we were in company. We talk all day long, I believe—talking to each other is just a livelier, more audible form of thinking. All my confidence is given to him; all his confidence is given to me. We are exactly suited in character—perfect harmony is the result.

Mr. Rochester continued to be blind for the first two years of our marriage. Perhaps it was that circumstance that drew us so close—that bound us so tightly. For I was then his eyes, as I am still his right hand. Literally, I was—as he often called me—the apple of his eye. He saw nature and books through me, and I never tired of gazing on his behalf and putting into words what I saw—field, tree, town, river, cloud, sunbeam—the landscape before us, the weather around us—and impressing by sound on his ear what light could no longer stamp upon his eyes. Never did I tire of reading to him; never did I tire of leading him wherever he wished to go, of doing for him whatever he wished done. And there was a pleasure in serving him, full and exquisite, even though tinged with sadness—because he accepted these services without painful shame or crushing humiliation. He loved me so truly that he felt no reluctance in relying on my care; he knew I loved him so fondly that to give that care was to indulge my dearest wishes.
One morning, at the end of those two years, as I was writing a letter to his dictation, he came and bent over me and said: "Jane, have you a glittering ornament around your neck?"
I had a gold watch chain. I answered "Yes."
"And have you a pale blue dress on?"
And have you a pale blue dress on?
I had. He told me then that for some time he had thought the darkness clouding one eye was becoming less dense. Now he was sure of it.

He and I went to London. He consulted an eminent eye specialist and eventually recovered the sight of that one eye. He cannot see very clearly now. He cannot read or write much. But he can find his way without being led by the hand. The sky is no longer a blank to him—the earth no longer a void. When his firstborn was placed in his arms, he could see that the boy had inherited his own eyes, as they once were—large, brilliant, and dark. On that occasion, he acknowledged once more, with a full heart, that God had tempered judgment with mercy.

My Edward and I are happy. And the more so because those we love most are happy too. Diana and Mary Rivers are both married. They visit us once a year, and we visit them. Diana's husband is a captain in the navy—a brave officer and a good man. Mary's is a clergyman, a college friend of her brother's, and worthy of the connection in every respect. Both Captain Fitzjames and Mr. Wharton love their wives and are loved by them.

As for St. John Rivers, he left England. He went to India. He entered on the path he had chosen for himself, and he follows it still. A more determined, tireless pioneer never struggled through hardship and danger. Firm, faithful, and devoted, full of energy, zeal, and truth, he works for humanity. He clears their painful way toward progress. He cuts down prejudices of creed and caste like a giant felling trees. He may be stern. He may be demanding. He may be ambitious still. But his is the sternness of the warrior Greatheart, who guards his pilgrim convoy from the onslaught of Apollyon. His is the demandingness of the apostle who speaks only for Christ, when he says—"Whoever wants to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me." His is the ambition of the great master-spirit who aims to take his place among the first rank of those redeemed from the earth—who stand without fault before the throne of God, who share the Lamb's last great victories, who are called, and chosen, and faithful.

St. John is unmarried. He never will marry now. He has been enough, by himself, for the work. And the work draws near its end. His glorious sun is hastening toward its setting. The last letter I received from him drew human tears from my eyes yet filled my heart with divine joy. He anticipated his sure reward—his imperishable crown. I know that a stranger's hand will write to me next, to say that the good and faithful servant has been called at last into the joy of his Lord. And why weep for this? No fear of death will darken St. John's last hour. His mind will be unclouded, his heart will be unshaken, his hope will be sure, his faith will be steadfast. His own words are a pledge of this—
"My Master," he says, "has forewarned me. Daily He announces more distinctly—'Surely I come quickly!' and hourly I more eagerly respond—'Amen; even so, come, Lord Jesus!'"
